interest: Henry W. Kinney, Japan's American publicist, suspected as a spy in Tahiti.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.20251M) contains despatches, diplomatic instructions, interdepartmental correspondence, and documentary enclosures from March 1941 to April 1942 concerning Henry Walsworth Kinney, an American journalist, author, and former Hawaii public official residing in Tahiti who was suspected of being an espionage and intelligence agent for the Japanese government in French Oceania. Initiated by reports from the American Consulate in Tahiti, the file traces an investigation involving the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Division of European Affairs, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation under J. Edgar Hoover. The documents explore Kinney's decades-long employment as chief publicist and propagandist for the South Manchuria Railway Company, his 1937–1938 work for the Japanese Foreign Office, his travels between Tokyo and Washington, and his wartime surveillance and interrogation by American Consul R. M. de Lambert following the outbreak of the Pacific War, supplemented by his own detailed autobiographical statement and book excerpts documenting both his propaganda writing and the pro-Japanese activities of his estranged son, Charles Bishop Kinney.

subfiles.about: Comprehensive consular report on Henry W. Kinney and his Japanese wife in Tahiti following the outbreak of war with Japan.
subfiles.from: R. M. de Lambert, American Consul, Tahiti
subfiles.summary: American Consul R. M. de Lambert reports on Henry Walsworth Kinney's situation in Tahiti following the outbreak of the Pacific War in December 1941. While local Japanese nationals have been interned at Taravao or restricted to phosphate mining on Makatea, Kinney and his Japanese wife remain free under suspicion at their Mataiea estate, though their radio receiver was confiscated by colonial authorities. De Lambert details Kinney's background, his written questionnaire responses, his estrangement from his son Charles Bishop Kinney (a South Manchuria Railway publicist in Manchuria), and his past propaganda writings for Japan.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 16 from Consul de Lambert (Tahiti) on Wartime Surveillance of Henry W. Kinney

subfiles.about: Detailed fifteen-point autobiographical questionnaire completed by Henry W. Kinney detailing his career, publicity work for Japan, and personal affairs.
subfiles.summary: Kinney's questionnaire answers defend his publicity work for Japan, deny espionage and describe his family.
subfiles.title: Statement and Questionnaire Responses by Henry W. Kinney Regarding His Career and Japanese Connections
subfiles.to: R. M. de Lambert, American Consul, Tahiti
